stories.headline: Sydney police step up armed patrols after Bondi terror attack
stories.title: Sydney police step up armed patrols after Bondi terror attack
stories.summary: Sydney, Oct 8 : Heavily armed police will be deployed across Australia's Sydney ahead of a rapid response unit established in the wake of the Bondi Beach terror attack becoming fully operational. The government of the Australian state of New South Wales (NSW) on Thursday said that officers from the state police force's new Armed Response Command (ARC) will begin patrolling Sydney over the coming weeks as the unit's training moves into realistic environments. The ARC was established as a permanent unit by the state government following the fatal mass shooting of 15 people at a Jewish holiday celebration at Bondi Beach in December last year, Xinhua News Agency reported. NSW Premier Chris Minns, Police and Counter-terrorism Minister Yasmin Catley and Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon said in a statement on Thursday that ARC officers will patrol high-risk areas, including places of worship and major events, and rapidly respond to emerging threats. The 250-officer unit will have access to combat assault rifles and 24 purpose-built vehicles and will be supported by a specialised operations centre. "Keeping the people of New South Wales safe is our number one priority. That means making sure our police have the people, training and equipment they need to respond to serious threats," Minns said. Lanyon said that the ARC would act as a deterrent for anyone who wishes to commit harm, incite hatred or cause fear. In February, accused Bondi Beach terror attack perpetrator Naveed Akram made his first appearance in a Sydney court after being charged with 59 offences over the fatal mass shooting. Akram appeared on Monday morning via video link from a supermax prison where he has been held since being discharged from the hospital in the wake of the attack on December 14, 2025. The 24-year-old was charged with 59 offences, including 15 counts of murder and one count of committing a terrorist act, in relation to the attack. Authorities allege that Akram and his father, Sajid, who was shot dead by police at the scene of the attack, opened fire on a Jewish celebration at the iconic eastern Sydney beach using rifles and shotguns, killing 15 people and injuring dozens more. Court documents made public in December 2025 revealed that police found evidence that the two attackers had conducted firearms training at a rural property before the attack. Local media reported that Akram was mostly silent during the administrative hearing and only spoke when directly addressed by the presiding Magistrate. --IANS

stories.headline: Mint Explainer | Why is Elon Musk’s Starlink at war with Indian telecom giants?
stories.title: Mint Explainer | Why is Elon Musk’s Starlink at war with Indian telecom giants?
stories.summary: Elon Musk claims Indian ‘oligarchs’ are stalling Starlink’s launch, deepening a fierce battle with Jio and Airtel over spectrum allocation and market control.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: On Wednesday, a post from SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk, who has 241.6 million followers on X, sparked a new battle involving the satellite firm, the Indian telecom sector, and the government.

Musk alleged that Indian “oligarchs” were scuttling Starlink’s launch in the country to maintain a “monopolistic chokehold on the Indian people.” While he named no individuals or companies, the troika commanding the Indian telecom industry comprises Reliance Jio Infocomm, Bharti Airtel, and Vodafone Idea.
By Thursday morning, the government refuted any suggestions of bias as “baseless and misconceived”.
Mint explains the satellite wars now engulfing India’s telecom industry.
How did the battle lines get drawn?

Starlink registered its business in India in 2021 and began advertising and preselling its services until the government stepped in, saying the company lacked a license and could not presell satellite connections without regulatory approval.
That marked the start of a long-drawn-out war between the US firm and its Indian rivals.
Starlink reapplied for the license in 2022 and eventually secured it last year.
OneWeb India was the first to receive the global mobile personal communications by satellite (GMPCS) licence in April 2022, followed by Jio Satellite in October 2022, and Starlink in June 2025.

More than four years after India issued the first license for satellite internet services, commercial launches for all players remain stalled due to security concerns and mistrust surrounding foreign satellite operators.
What is stalling approvals for satellite operators?
Awaiting the final nod are Elon Musk-owned Starlink, Bharti-backed Eutelsat OneWeb, and Jio Satellite Communications Ltd, a wholly owned subsidiary of Jio Platforms.

stories.headline: Entire texture of CM Vijay’s election case changed, says Madras High Court Judge
stories.title: Entire texture of CM Vijay’s election case changed, says Madras High Court Judge
stories.summary: Justice V. Lakshminarayanan wants to know how Mr. Vijay would overcome the Supreme Court rulings on the subject
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in summary weight 26.4
article_sentences: The hearing on Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay’s plea to reject an election petition filed against his victory from the Perambur constituency took an interesting turn on Wednesday (October 7, 2026), with Justice V. Lakshminarayanan of the Madras High Court remarking that the entire texture of the case had changed in view of the Supreme Court judgments cited by counsel for the election petitioner.

After hearing the arguments made on behalf of the Chief Minister on Monday and Tuesday, the Judge began firing a volley of questions at the election petitioner’s counsel on Wednesday (October 7, 2026), asking how some alleged discrepancies in assets worth over ₹600 crore declared by Mr. Vijay would amount to undue influence over voters or could be termed as a corrupt electoral practice.

The Judge wanted to know whether the voters in the Perambur constituency would have been swayed in one direction or the other simply because there was a difference of a few crores or a few lakhs in the assets declared by the Chief Minister, especially in light of the fact that he was a “superstar” in the cinema industry and had voluntarily declared both movable and immovable properties worth more than ₹600 crore.
The Judge said he had relied on a chartered accountant to declare his assets while being elevated to the position of a Judge of the High Court.

Therefore, if Mr. Vijay had also declared his assets through a chartered accountant, how could his election itself be declared null and void for any mistakes made by the auditor in such a declaration, the Judge wondered.

He also questioned the challenge made by a voter, S. Dinesh, through his counsel on record, V.R. Shanmuganathan, to the election of the Chief Minister from Perambur on the ground of improper acceptance of the nomination form by the Returning Officer concerned.
The Judge wanted to know how the Returning Officer could be expected to verify the correctness of the declared assets.

In answering the questions, the election petitioner’s counsel said that the Returning Officer was expected to conduct only a summary inquiry, whereas the charge of false declaration, and whether such declaration was made wilfully and deliberately, could be inquired into only by means of leading evidence during the course of trial in an election petition.
Hence, the election petition should not be rejected at the threshold, he argued.

He said, Justice V. Ramasubramanian (during his stint in the Madras High Court before his retirement as a Supreme Court Judge) had in Krishnamoorthy versus Sivakumar (2009) held that “any incorrect information, wrong information, incomplete information, false information, one-sided information, disinformation, misinformation and non-information would certainly interfere with the free exercise of the electoral right of the voter, inasmuch as his choice of candidate will be influenced greatly by the information so furnished or withheld.”
“The view taken by Justice Ramasubramanian was affirmed by the Supreme Court in 2015.
Therefore, I have made out a cause of action for the trial of the election petition and it should not be rejected in limine,” the counsel said.

stories.headline: Explosions are heard in Saudi capital as Riyadh airport is reported closed
stories.title: Explosions are heard in Saudi capital as Riyadh airport is reported closed
stories.summary: Cairo, Oct 8: Several explosions were heard in Saudi Arabia's capital of Riyadh on Thursday, including a large blast at the city's international airport, a witness told The Associated Press, a day after the kingdom said an attack there killed one person and wounded others. The cause of the blasts was not immediately known. There was no immediate claim of responsibility. Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighbouring Yemen have repeatedly claimed attacks against airports, military and oil facilities in Saudi Arabia in recent days. The blasts had an immediate effect on markets and oil prices as the price of crude jumped. King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh “closed again,” the Flightradar24 monitor said Thursday on X. “Last landing 80+ minutes ago. Last take off 90+ minutes ago.” Fire and ambulance crews were deployed and smoke was visible, the witness said, speaking on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to speak to the media. The witness said outgoing flights were halted and passengers were instructed to leave all checked-in luggage behind and evacuate the airport. It was not immediately clear how many flights were disrupted. Saudi authorities did not respond to requests for comment. On Wednesday, Saudi officials said two attacks on airports claimed by the Houthis had killed three people, as the kingdom was pulled deeper into the latest front in the Iran war. The attack on King Khalid airport killed a Sudanese national and wounded eight other people, and the attack on Abha airport killed Moroccan and Algerian residents and wounded 28 others, officials said. Attacks on the kingdom, the world's top oil exporter, have raised alarm. Over the weekend, Saudi Arabia and allied Yemeni forces launched a major ground and air offensive aimed at retaking territory that the Houthis seized a month ago along Yemen's western Red Sea coast and on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The rebels' presence on the waterway poses a threat to the crucial shipping alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where traffic has been curtailed due to the Iran war. Also Wednesday, the spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis, Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki, said forces destroyed a platform in Yemen's rebel-held capital of Sanaa that had been used to launch attacks on the Saudi capital. The AP could not independently verify these claims. (AP)

stories.headline: Microfinance's reckoning: Can India's lenders grow without repeating the past?
stories.title: Microfinance's reckoning: Can India's lenders grow without repeating the past?
stories.summary: For years, India's microfinance industry ran on the formula of lending small amounts to millions of low-income households, keeping collections high, adding borrowers and branches and letting scale do the rest. The model made microfinance one of the country's most important channels of formal credit for households conventional banks found too expensive to serve.After surviving the Covid-19 pandemic, the industry entered the post-pandemic period with confidence. Demand returned strongly, capital was plentiful, new players entered and competition for borrowers intensified. “Microfinance institutions were mono-line businesses for a long time due to regulatory prescription," says Ganesh Narayanan, CEO and MD of CreditAccess Grameen. The problem was not just an external shock hitting an otherwise sound business; it was perhaps the first time, the sector itself had begun to overheat.Lenders competed for customers already borrowing from several institutions, and indebtedness accumulated beneath what still looked like healthy growth. At the peak, around a quarter of CreditAccess Grameen's AUM was linked to borrowers with exposure to more than three lenders; that figure is now around 2 percent.The warning signs were visible in credit-bureau data, but the industry was slow to act. When collections deteriorated in 2024, the first explanations were external—heat waves, elections, campaigns against indebtedness.Then came the Karza Mukti Abhiyan and legislative intervention, most notably in Karnataka. What looked like temporary disturbances exposed a deeper vulnerability: Credit had grown faster than the industry's ability to assess a household's total repayment capacity. However, not all credit stress is the same. A borrower hit by a drought can recover once the shock passes; a household that has taken on debt beyond what it can service faces a different problem entirely.The industry spent much of the downturn figuring out which it was dealing with. By the time leverage emerged as the bigger issue, lenders were already facing higher credit costs, weaker collections, tighter funding and a sceptical investor base.In response, underwriting tightened, scrutiny of household indebtedness increased, and borrower-level monitoring strengthened. By mid-2026, around 98 percent of borrowers were within the industry's lender-count limits meaning no borrower can borrow from more than three lenders.ICRA reports a meaningful reduction in overleveraging—95 percent of borrowers now have exposure to three lenders or fewer. It expects assets under management growth to rebound to 15-17 per cent in FY27. But with cleaner credit metrics, can these businesses generate attractive returns without eventually recreating the same problem?With a bit of caution in mind, Gautam Trivedi, co-founder and managing partner at Nepean Capital, says, "We will stay away from these stocks.” In his view, some of the industry's difficulties are structural rather than cyclical—borrowers stacking multiple loans, weak enforceability, and the risk of legislative intervention, like Karnataka showed.Also Read: How No-Cost-EMIs have changed the way Indians shopBorrowers Still ExistIndia's low-income households still need working capital, emergency finance, and money for housing and small businesses.Moneylenders still operate alongside formal institutions, proof that demand in this segment far exceeds what the formal MFI industry serves. Venkatesh Krishnan, CEO of Spandana Sphoorty, believes this is why microfinance will remain relevant for decades. What has changed is the borrower. A customer who enters the system with a Rs 30,000 joint-liability loan won't stay a microfinance customer forever.As income and business needs grow, so does demand. For the lender, instead of constantly acquiring new borrowers, it can retain the ones it already knows and grow the relationship.The scale of that opportunity shows at CreditAccess Grameen. Its existing customers have borrowed roughly Rs 83,000 crore from other lenders while its own "graduation" portfolio—where customers borrow outside of microfinance—is only around Rs 5,600 crore as of June 2026.This implies that the industry's future may lie less in finding millions of new borrowers than in following existing customers as their needs evolve. That's a reshaping strategy, rather than staying pure-play joint-liability lenders, MFIs want to become broader financial-services companies serving the same customer across life stages.Regulation has helped too. In June 2025, the RBI cut the qualifying-asset requirement for NBFC-MFIs from 75 percent to 60 percent of total assets, giving them room to diversify. This means that lenders can now have 40 percent of their loans outside microfinance compared to 25 percent earlier.CreditAccess Grameen wants roughly half its business from non-MFI activities by 2031, with 20-30 percent of its portfolio in secured loans. Spandana is keeping joint-liability lending as its core while expanding individual loans and loans against property.Across the sector, lenders are talking about migrating customers to secured products and using data to spot borrowers capable of larger loans. The challenge is distinguishing a borrower whose income has genuinely grown from one whose apparent capacity simply reflects more debt. That may be the central lesson of the downturn: growth alone is no longer enough.Also Read: Why retailers love buy now, pay laterThe Economics Have To ChangeThe real test now isn't whether loan growth returns. It’s whether lenders can grow while producing acceptable returns through an entire credit cycle, a much higher bar than before.The numbers offer a sobering baseline. According to Alok Misra, CEO of the Micro Finance Industry Network (MFIN), the top 15 microfinance companies generated average ROA of about 2.2 percent and ROE of roughly 8.5 percent between 2016 and 2024—a period that includes Covid's disruption.MFIN believes a well-run microfinance business should generate around 3.5 percent ROA and 15-16 percent return on equity over a cycle. Returns of 20-22 percent, while possible in good years, are unlikely to be sustainable without taking on more risk.That creates a balancing act. The strongest players have spent years building distribution networks and field forces that are valuable but operationally heavy.With pricing competitive and credit costs still elevated, margin is limited, and charging borrowers more isn't really an option. Even though pricing has been deregulated, it stays politically sensitive. The more durable path is improving productivity, using technology better, and deepening each customer relationship—which is where diversification comes in.The RBI's June 2025 rule change lets lenders hold up to 40 percent of their books outside microfinance, effectively turning microfinance into a customer-acquisition engine rather than the whole business.Gold loans, individual loans, housing finance and MSME lending offer larger ticket sizes and different risk profiles, reducing the earnings volatility of relying almost entirely on unsecured group lending.For bigger players, even a modest slice of a large balance sheet can be meaningful. CreditAccess Grameen's historical ROA has swung between 4-5 percent in good years and 1-2 percent in bad ones; the ambition behind its diversification push is a more consistent cross-cycle 4 percent.Another lesson that may matter as much as diversification is that the industry needs to know exactly who it's lending to. The multiple-lending problem was partly a failure of borrower identification."The need for a unique identifier is very important," says Baskar Babu R, MD of Suryoday Small Finance Bank. The industry is moving towards PAN and CKYC as the only acceptable borrower identifiers.The Road AheadFunding may determine which lenders emerge strongest. The crisis exposed a clear divide between institutions with strong balance sheets and smaller players that struggled to raise money.A government-backed Rs 20,000 crore credit guarantee scheme has helped. Industry estimates suggest around Rs 450 crore of funding has been facilitated for 25-30 smaller institutions. It doesn't solve the funding problem outright, but it gives banks more comfort at a time when their appetite for MFI exposure has fallen.That imbalance could accelerate consolidation, as smaller MFIs decide whether to raise expensive capital, sell, or become business correspondents for larger lenders. But similar predictions were made during earlier funding crises, and pure-play MFIs didn't disappear then either. As of July, NBFC-MFIs accounted for about 45 percent of the market as per MFIN data, against 23 percent for banks.Even if every MFI follows its guardrails, the same customer can still borrow from a fintech, NBFC or bank outside the MFI framework, or from informal lenders outside the bureau system entirely and this remains an unsolved problem. That's why a unique identifier and cross-lender coordination matter as much as any single lender's discipline.Political risk is the other uncomfortable variable. The past two years showed how quickly borrower distress can turn political, and how a state government's intervention can reshape an entire industry's operating environment, a key reason for scepticism like Trivedi's."The learnings of this crisis will stay for long," says Babu. If memories fade as growth accelerates, the next cycle could resemble the last one. Meanwhile, for investors, proof will come through numbers, not promises—credit costs normalising, ROE moving toward sustainable levels, and growth returning without another rise in borrower leverage.

The industry spent much of the downturn figuring out which it was dealing with.
By the time leverage emerged as the bigger issue, lenders were already facing higher credit costs, weaker collections, tighter funding and a sceptical investor base.
In response, underwriting tightened, scrutiny of household indebtedness increased, and borrower-level monitoring strengthened.
It expects assets under management growth to rebound to 15-17 per cent in FY27.
But with cleaner credit metrics, can these businesses generate attractive returns without eventually recreating the same problem?

With a bit of caution in mind, Gautam Trivedi, co-founder and managing partner at Nepean Capital, says, "We will stay away from these stocks.” In his view, some of the industry's difficulties are structural rather than cyclical—borrowers stacking multiple loans, weak enforceability, and the risk of legislative intervention, like Karnataka showed.
Borrowers Still Exist.
India's low-income households still need working capital, emergency finance, and money for housing and small businesses.
Moneylenders still operate alongside formal institutions, proof that demand in this segment far exceeds what the formal MFI industry serves.
Venkatesh Krishnan, CEO of Spandana Sphoorty, believes this is why microfinance will remain relevant for decades.
What has changed is the borrower.
A customer who enters the system with a Rs 30,000 joint-liability loan won't stay a microfinance customer forever.
As income and business needs grow, so does demand.
For the lender, instead of constantly acquiring new borrowers, it can retain the ones it already knows and grow the relationship.
The scale of that opportunity shows at CreditAccess Grameen.

Its existing customers have borrowed roughly Rs 83,000 crore from other lenders while its own "graduation" portfolio—where customers borrow outside of microfinance—is only around Rs 5,600 crore as of June 2026.
This implies that the industry's future may lie less in finding millions of new borrowers than in following existing customers as their needs evolve.
That's a reshaping strategy, rather than staying pure-play joint-liability lenders, MFIs want to become broader financial-services companies serving the same customer across life stages.
Regulation has helped too.
In June 2025, the RBI cut the qualifying-asset requirement for NBFC-MFIs from 75 percent to 60 percent of total assets, giving them room to diversify.
Spandana is keeping joint-liability lending as its core while expanding individual loans and loans against property.
Across the sector, lenders are talking about migrating customers to secured products and using data to spot borrowers capable of larger loans.
The challenge is distinguishing a borrower whose income has genuinely grown from one whose apparent capacity simply reflects more debt.
That may be the central lesson of the downturn: growth alone is no longer enough.
The Economics Have To Change.
The real test now isn't whether loan growth returns.
It’s whether lenders can grow while producing acceptable returns through an entire credit cycle, a much higher bar than before.
The numbers offer a sobering baseline.

According to Alok Misra, CEO of the Micro Finance Industry Network (MFIN), the top 15 microfinance companies generated average ROA of about 2.2 percent and ROE of roughly 8.5 percent between 2016 and 2024—a period that includes Covid's disruption.
Returns of 20-22 percent, while possible in good years, are unlikely to be sustainable without taking on more risk.
That creates a balancing act.
The strongest players have spent years building distribution networks and field forces that are valuable but operationally heavy.
With pricing competitive and credit costs still elevated, margin is limited, and charging borrowers more isn't really an option.
Even though pricing has been deregulated, it stays politically sensitive.
The more durable path is improving productivity, using technology better, and deepening each customer relationship—which is where diversification comes in.

Gold loans, individual loans, housing finance and MSME lending offer larger ticket sizes and different risk profiles, reducing the earnings volatility of relying almost entirely on unsecured group lending.
For bigger players, even a modest slice of a large balance sheet can be meaningful.
Another lesson that may matter as much as diversification is that the industry needs to know exactly who it's lending to.
The multiple-lending problem was partly a failure of borrower identification." The need for a unique identifier is very important," says Baskar Babu R, MD of Suryoday Small Finance Bank.
The industry is moving towards PAN and CKYC as the only acceptable borrower identifiers.
The Road AheadFunding may determine which lenders emerge strongest.
The crisis exposed a clear divide between institutions with strong balance sheets and smaller players that struggled to raise money.
A government-backed Rs 20,000 crore credit guarantee scheme has helped.
Industry estimates suggest around Rs 450 crore of funding has been facilitated for 25-30 smaller institutions.
It doesn't solve the funding problem outright, but it gives banks more comfort at a time when their appetite for MFI exposure has fallen.
That imbalance could accelerate consolidation, as smaller MFIs decide whether to raise expensive capital, sell, or become business correspondents for larger lenders.
But similar predictions were made during earlier funding crises, and pure-play MFIs didn't disappear then either.

Even if every MFI follows its guardrails, the same customer can still borrow from a fintech, NBFC or bank outside the MFI framework, or from informal lenders outside the bureau system entirely and this remains an unsolved problem.
That's why a unique identifier and cross-lender coordination matter as much as any single lender's discipline.
Political risk is the other uncomfortable variable.

The past two years showed how quickly borrower distress can turn political, and how a state government's intervention can reshape an entire industry's operating environment, a key reason for scepticism like Trivedi's." The learnings of this crisis will stay for long," says Babu.
If memories fade as growth accelerates, the next cycle could resemble the last one.
Meanwhile, for investors, proof will come through numbers, not promises—credit costs normalising, ROE moving toward sustainable levels, and growth returning without another rise in borrower leverage.

stories.headline: Police register FIR to probe violence during CJP's July 20 protest
stories.title: Police register FIR to probe violence during CJP's July 20 protest
stories.summary: The Crime Branch of the Delhi Police has registered an FIR to investigate the violence that broke out during the Cockroach Janta Party's (CJP) protest in the national capital on July 20, police sources said on Thursday. The probe will focus on identifying people allegedly responsible for the violence and examine whether it was premeditated, the sources said. On the directions of the Supreme Court, the Delhi Police had cancelled 17 FIRs registered at multiple police stations in the New Delhi district. The FIR comes two days ahead of another CJP protest announced to be held at Jantar Mantar, this time to press for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the SIR exercise. A police officer said that permission has not been granted for any protest. Referring to the fresh FIR, the police source told PTI that teams of the Crime Branch will also look into whether criminal elements entered the protest sites after the CJP called for a march

stories.headline: CAPF Act that governs officer posts, deputation comes into force
stories.title: CAPF Act that governs officer posts, deputation comes into force
stories.summary: New Delhi, Oct 8: The Central Armed Police Forces (General Administration) Act, 2026, which provides a common framework for recruitment and conditions of service of Group-A general duty officers and other officers in the CAPFs, came into force on Thursday, according a government notification. The notification came at a time when the Supreme Court is hearing a bunch of petitions filed by thousands of CAPF officers challenging the validity of the law that was passed by the Parliament in April. "In exercise of the powers conferred by sub-section (2) of section 1 of the Central Armed Police Forces (General Administration) Act, 2026, the Central Government hereby appoints the 08th day of October, 2026, as the date on which the provisions of the said Act shall come into force," said the notification issued by the Ministry of Home Affairs. The CAPF Act provides for regulation of recruitment, promotion, deputation and other conditions of service of officers in the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF), Border Security Force (BSF), Central Industrial Security Force (CISF), Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) and Sashastra Seema Bal (SSB). The Centre recently told the apex court through an affidavit that the appointment of Group 'A' general duty officers in the respective CAPFs is now regulated by the CAPF (General Administration) Act. It had said that the Act "expressly empowers" the Central government to prescribe the method, manner and mode of recruitment, including by deputation, and the conditions of service of officers in the five CAPFs-- CRPF, BSF, CISF, ITBP and SSB. The cadre officers of these forces have petitioned the top court, including by filing a contempt petition, that the Act continues to restrict their career progression in comparison to the Indian Police Service (IPS) officers brought on deputation. They have also asked the apex court to direct the Union government to implement its May 2025 judgement that said that the deputation of IPS officers up to the rank of inspector general in the CAPFs should be "progressively reduced" over a period of two years in order to give more opportunities to cadre officers whose delayed promotions can "adversely" impact the morale of these forces. Under the new legislation, 50 per cent of the posts in the rank of inspector general are to be filled through deputation from the IPS, while a minimum of 67 per cent of posts at the additional director general level are to be filled through deputation. The posts in the ranks of special director general and director general are to be filled through deputation only. The Act comes against the backdrop of the Supreme Court's May 2025 judgment on the deputation of IPS officers in the CAPFs. In October last year, the apex court dismissed the Centre’s plea seeking a review of its 2025 verdict. The court had said the number of posts earmarked for deputation in CAPF cadres up to the SAG level should be progressively reduced over a period of time, with an outer limit of two years, and had directed a cadre review. The Statement of Objects and Reasons of the legislation said the expanding functional and operational requirements of the CAPFs had resulted in a distinct organisational structure for the forces. "In recent years, due to the absence of an umbrella law, regulatory provisions have evolved in a fragmented manner, resulting in several litigation on service-related matters, leading to some functional and administrative difficulties," it said. The law replaces the fragmented framework governing service matters with a common legislative framework for Group-A general duty officers and other officers in the five CAPFs. A group of retired CAPF officers had also approached the Supreme Court with a contempt plea against then Home Secretary Govind Mohan over alleged non-implementation of the apex court's October 2025 order. The group had said any legislative intervention affecting the command structure, service conditions and leadership opportunities within the CAPFs would have implications for institutional morale and the operational effectiveness of forces responsible for internal security and border security.

stories.headline: Supreme Court directs Udayasthamana pooja to be held as per Guruvayur temple practices
stories.title: Supreme Court directs Udayasthamana pooja to be held as per Guruvayur temple practices
stories.summary: A Bench headed by Justice Aravind Kumar said the interim order prioritises the faith and sentiments of worshippers over management hurdles
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Thursday (October 8, 2026) passed an interim order that the Udayasthamana Pooja must be held in accordance with the age-old practices of the famed Guruvayur Sri Krishna Temple in Keralam.
A Bench headed by Justice Aravind Kumar remarked the faith and sentiments of worshippers must be given precedence over management hurdles.

The petitioners led by P.C. Hary and members of traditional managing families, represented by senior advocate Guru Krishnakumar, had challenged decisions by the Guruvayur devaswom managing committee to alter or reschedule the Udayasthamana Pooja on Vrishchikam Ekadasi.

The management, represented by senior advocates CA Sundaram, V. Giri and advocate Rohini Musa, had argued that the performance of the rituals during Ekadasi was faced by logistical challenges posed by the massive influx of devotees on that particular day.
“I have myself stood for seven hours,” Justice Kumar said, indicating it was part of the devotional expression.
The court said it would list the main appeal in December for final hearing.

The petitioners had moved the apex court after the Kerala High Court had dismissed their pleas for a direction to the temple devaswom to ensure the conduct of the Udayasthamana pooja on Vrishchikam Ekadasi.
In October last year, the apex court had passed a similar order allowing the conduct of the pooja on the Ekadasi day which fell in the month of November.
Mr. Hary had argued that the pooja was a sacred and integral part of the temple’s ritualistic tradition.

“Until 2023, the Udayasthamana pooja was invariably performed on Vrishchikam Ekadasi day, and it is only during the last two years, 2024 and 2025, that the respondents have attempted to alter this well-established religious practice.
Such arbitrary decisions by the respondents strike at the very root of the traditional practices of the temple, which have been observed for several centuries.
The Udayasthamana pooja on Vrishchikam Ekadasi is not merely symbolic but a series of nearly 15-18 poojas that are conducted from sunrise to sunset,” the petitioners had submitted.

stories.headline: Supreme Court Questions Jharkhand DGP Appointment Rule, Asks Amicus To Examine Validity Of Other States' Rules
stories.title: Supreme Court Questions Jharkhand DGP Appointment Rule, Asks Amicus To Examine Validity Of Other States' Rules
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: In the Jharkhand DGP Appointment case, the Supreme Court today passed an order calling on Amicus Curiae, Senior Advocate Raju Ramachandran, to examine the statutes/rules pertaining to DGP appointments in other states.

A bench of CJI Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V Mohana prima facie observed that a 2025 Jharkhand rule, which allowed an officer with residual service of less than 6 months before superannuation to be considered for DGP Appointment, was contrary to the law laid down by the Court in Prakash Singh case.
It was referring to the rule contained in Selection and Appointment of Director General and Inspector General of Police, Jharkhand (Head of Police Force) Regulations, 2025.
Considering that annulment of the rule could affect the appointment of Jharkhand DGP, Smt Tadasha Mishra, it issued notice to Mishra, so she can have an opportunity of being heard.
The bench also said that in the meantime, Jharkhand government may revisit the offending rule.
In the alternative, it may file a counter-affidavit.
"Such provision prima facie seems to be directly in teeth of law laid down in Prakash Singh.
In the event of the rule being annulled, appointment of Smt.
Tadasha Mishra, DGP of Jharkhand, would be required to be set aside.
We therefore deem it apt.
